tagline: A mountain road climbs through cliffs, aspens and lava toward Panguitch.
intro: Utah’s Patchwork Parkway climbs from Parowan through red and white cliffs, then crosses high country before descending through aspens and lava fields to Panguitch. Visit Utah gives the drive as 50 miles and 1.5 hours, highlighting the changing cliffs, forests, meadows and lakes along SR 143. It became a National Scenic Byway in 2009.

The western road began as a wagon route built by Mormon settlers to reach timber above Parowan. S. A. Halterman drove an automobile to Cedar Breaks through the canyon in 1919; improvements allowed him to take visitors weekly by 1921. SR 143 was commissioned in 1933, and its extension to Panguitch came in 1985. The initial state route stopped at the Dixie National Forest boundary. A 1953 extension took the designation to Cedar Breaks’ north boundary, before the later addition of Panguitch Lake Road.

The Patchwork name recalls an earlier mountain crossing for food. After frost killed most of Panguitch’s first settlers’ crops, seven men set out for supplies. They reportedly laid quilts on the snow to keep from sinking after abandoning their wagons.
From Parowan, climb past Brian Head to Cedar Breaks’ North View. Turn east through the aspen and lava country to Panguitch Lake, then follow pastures and Panguitch Creek into Panguitch.

moments.title: Cedar Breaks National Monument
moments.text: At Cedar Breaks, erosion has cut a natural amphitheater three miles across and more than 2,000 feet deep. SR 143 passes its North View before meeting SR 148. The canyon’s shale, limestone and sandstone began as deposits in ancient Lake Claron. Uplift raised those layers, and erosion wore them away over millions of years. Iron oxides give the rock reds, oranges and yellows; manganese oxides contribute purple. Above the canyon, bristlecone pines grow in the high country, including specimens more than 1,600 years old. Subalpine meadows also dot the rim, including the Alpine Pond area.
moments.notice: Look for red, orange and yellow rock colored by iron oxides, with purple from manganese oxides.

moments.title: Panguitch Lake
moments.text: Panguitch Lake was a natural lake before a 24-foot dam enlarged it into a reservoir. The original water covered 777 acres; the reservoir’s maximum surface area is 1,248 acres. It lies on the Markagunt Plateau between Cedar Breaks and Panguitch and drains into the Sevier River. The lake’s earliest known use was as a Paiute fishery, and its name means “big fish” in the Paiute language. SR 143 supplies road access to the lake, which the local tourism bureau identifies with fishing and boating. The lake lies within Dixie National Forest.

moments.title: Panguitch
moments.text: Rose-colored brick houses in Panguitch carry the story of wages paid in building material. Settlers fired local clay in kilns; workers used their brick pay to build homes. The historic district’s houses also reveal a local building pattern: many have square plans, pyramidal roofs and projecting bays. Most district residences date from 1890 to 1930. Many buildings use deep-red, soft-edged brick produced near Panguitch between 1915 and 1940, adding another chapter to the town’s use of local clay. At the Ira Hatch House, a square tower combines with a mix of Victorian Eclectic and Queen Anne details.
moments.notice: Look for brick houses with square plans, pyramidal roofs and projecting bays.

practical: Cedar Breaks National Monument: SR 148 generally closes from mid-November through late May. SR 143 between Brian Head and Panguitch is subject to bad-weather closures. The Parowan–Brian Head approach has grades reaching 13 percent and is not recommended for RVs or semi-trucks. (checked 2026-10-11)
